## Story

> Kleeberg's city library, after closing. Your evening tour of the archive had just begun when the fire-safety system sealed the door behind you.
>
> The archive's scripts belong to Margarete Holm, the archivist, who retired last week and left most of them half-finished. Above her desk hangs her rule: **"I never write down what the documentation already says."** Her notes only tell you where to look.
>
> So look: the official Python documentation is open in another tab of your browser, and the handbook on the reading stand links to its main pages. Use the docs for Python 3.14, the version this archive runs.

## Stations

### 1. Returns cart

**Practises:** Reading a HOWTO: Python's sort is stable, so a sort on two keys in opposite directions is two sorts, the secondary key first.  
**Needs:** 🔎 Note on the returns cart  
**Data:** [cart.py](../../content/rooms/python-docs/data/cart.py)

**Task:**

> A cart full of returned books stands by the shelves, its brake locked until the books are in Margarete's shelving order.
>
> The books are loaded as `returns`, a list of dictionaries with `"title"` and `"shelf"`. Store the titles in shelving order in `cart`, a list of strings.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
# returns is loaded: a list of dicts with "title" and "shelf".
print(returns[0])

cart = []  # the titles, in shelving order
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
by_title = sorted(returns, key=lambda b: b["title"], reverse=True)
by_shelf = sorted(by_title, key=lambda b: b["shelf"])
cart = [b["title"] for b in by_shelf]
print(cart)
```

**Checked result** (`cart`):

```json
["Winter Birds", "Apples of the Valley", "A Short History of Rain", "Kleeberg in Old Photographs", "Bridges", "Salt Roads", "Moss and Lichen", "Field Notes", "Paper Boats", "Northern Lights", "The Lantern Keeper", "The Clockmaker"]
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The brake clicks free. Taped under the handle is a tag: **returns → 7**

**Hints:**

1. Margarete's note on the cart gives the shelving order. The HOWTOs are linked from the docs' start page and from the handbook. In "Sorting Techniques", read the section "Sort Stability and Complex Sorts".
2. Sorts are stable: records with the same key keep their order. So sort by the secondary key first (title, `reverse=True`), then by the primary key (shelf).
3. `by_title = sorted(returns, key=lambda b: b["title"], reverse=True)`, then `sorted(by_title, key=lambda b: b["shelf"])`, then take the titles.

### 2. Packing table

**Practises:** Finding a function from a description: the module index, the overview at the top of a module's page, a signature's parameters.  
**Needs:** 🔎 Label on an archive box  
**Data:** [boxes.py](../../content/rooms/python-docs/data/boxes.py)

**Task:**

> A pile of books waits on the packing table to go down to the cellar, next to a stack of empty archive boxes. The cellar lift only takes full instructions: which books go into which box.
>
> The call numbers are loaded as `book_ids`. Pack them into boxes and store the boxes in `boxes`, a list with one tuple or list of call numbers per box.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
# book_ids is loaded: call numbers like "K-0412".
print(len(book_ids), book_ids[:3])

boxes = []
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
from itertools import batched

boxes = list(batched(sorted(book_ids), 7))
print(len(boxes), boxes[-1])
```

**Checked result** (`[list(b) for b in boxes]`):

```json
[["K-0017", "K-0026", "K-0083", "K-0108", "K-0125", "K-0194", "K-0251"], ["K-0277", "K-0312", "K-0349", "K-0372", "K-0412", "K-0487", "K-0561"], ["K-0590", "K-0640", "K-0698", "K-0733", "K-0759", "K-0815", "K-0866"], ["K-0904", "K-0938"]]
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The lift hums and takes the boxes down. A number is stamped on the last box's lid: **packing → 4**

**Hints:**

1. The label on the archive boxes says how to pack them. Open `itertools` from the module index. The tables at the top of its page list every function with a one-line description; one of them makes groups of a fixed size.
2. `itertools.batched(iterable, n)` gives tuples of `n` items; the last one may be shorter. It returns an iterator, so wrap it in `list(...)`. And the label wants call-number order first.
3. `from itertools import batched` and `boxes = list(batched(sorted(book_ids), 7))`

### 3. Late-fees ledger

**Practises:** Reading the notes under a function (`round()` rounds ties to even, floats aren't exact) and following the docs to another module (`decimal`, `quantize`, rounding modes).  
**Needs:** 🔎 Fee rules  
**Data:** [fees.py](../../content/rooms/python-docs/data/fees.py)

**Task:**

> The late-fees ledger never balanced: Margarete's fee script always came out a few cents off. A pencil note in the margin: "Why my script is wrong is written under `round()` in the built-in functions. Follow the docs from there."
>
> The ledger is loaded as `ledger`, a list of `(title, days overdue)` pairs. Work out every book's fee to the cent and store the sum in `total`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
# Margarete's fee script. ledger is loaded: (title, days overdue) pairs.
RATE = 0.0  # euros per day

total = 0
for title, days in ledger:
    fee = round(days * RATE, 2)
    total += fee
print(total)
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

RATE = Decimal("0.045")  # 4.5 cents per day

total = 0
for title, days in ledger:
    fee = (days * RATE).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
    total += fee
print(total)
```

**Checked result** (`str(total)`):

```json
"6.30"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The ledger balances to the cent. In the margin, in red ink: **fees → 1**

**Hints:**

1. The library's fee rules give the rate and how to round. Under `round()` the docs say two things: ties are rounded toward the even choice, and a float like `2.675` can't be stored exactly. The note there names the module for exact decimal arithmetic.
2. On the `decimal` page: build numbers from strings, `Decimal("0.045")`, not from floats; round each fee with `.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)`.
3. `from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP`, then in the loop `fee = (days * Decimal("0.045")).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)`.

### 4. The old terminal

**Practises:** Version notes: every entry in the docs says when it was added or changed ("Added in version 3.x"), so you know whether code runs on an older Python.  
**Needs:** 🔎 Margarete's script list

**Task:**

> The reading-room terminal is ancient. Its boot screen says `Python 3.8.10`. Margarete wanted to run her scripts on it.
>
> The terminal asks for its admin code: for every function her scripts use that doesn't exist yet in Python 3.8, the minor version of the Python release that added it, in the order she listed them, with no spaces. (A function added in Python 3.11 would give `11`.)

**Answer:** `91012`

**Reveals when solved:**

> The terminal beeps and prints a slip: "Stamp machine, service PIN: **5318**"

**Hints:**

1. Margarete pinned the list of functions next to the terminal. Look each one up (the general index or the search finds it). At the end of its entry there is a note such as "Added in version 3.x".
2. Functions added in 3.8 or earlier run on the terminal. Two of the five on the list do.
3. `str.removeprefix` 3.9, `math.dist` 3.8, `itertools.pairwise` 3.10, `statistics.fmean` 3.8, `itertools.batched` 3.12.

### 5. Date-stamp machine

**Practises:** Reading a table in the docs, and the notes under it: the `strftime` format codes, and why ISO week dates need `%G` with `%V` and `%u`.  
**Needs:** 🔒 4. The old terminal, 🔎 Stamp machine instructions  
**Data:** [stamps.py](../../content/rooms/python-docs/data/stamps.py)

**Code lock** (opens with `5318`):

> The stamp machine's cover is locked. A small display asks for a four-digit service PIN.

**Task:**

> The stamp machine prints a return stamp into every book. Its tray is full, but Margarete's stamp script prints nonsense around New Year.
>
> The return dates are loaded as `returned`, ISO date strings. Fix the script so that `stamps` holds the correct return stamp for every book.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
from datetime import date

# Margarete's stamp script. returned is loaded: ISO date strings like "2026-06-10".
stamps = []
for text in returned:
    day = date.fromisoformat(text)
    stamps.append(day.strftime("%Y-W%W-%w"))
print(stamps)
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
from datetime import date

stamps = []
for text in returned:
    day = date.fromisoformat(text)
    stamps.append(day.strftime("%G-W%V-%u"))
print(stamps)
```

**Checked result** (`stamps`):

```json
["2026-W01-1", "2026-W01-7", "2026-W11-7", "2026-W24-3", "2026-W53-4", "2026-W53-5", "2027-W01-1"]
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The machine stamps the last book and drops a brass token: **stamps → 8**

**Hints:**

1. The machine's instructions give the stamp format. On the `datetime` page, the section "strftime() and strptime() Format Codes" has a table of codes. Three of them mention ISO 8601.
2. `%V` is the ISO week, `%u` the ISO weekday (Monday is 1). The docs say the ISO year and week directives are not interchangeable with `%Y` and `%W`: around New Year the ISO year is `%G`.
3. `day.strftime("%G-W%V-%u")`

## Handbook in the room: 📖 How to read the Python docs

**Finding your way:** [`Library Reference`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/index.html), [`Module index`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/py-modindex.html), [`General index`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/genindex.html), [`Search`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/search.html), [`HOWTOs`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/index.html), [`Glossary`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/glossary.html)

**Reading an entry:** [`name(a, b=1, *, c=None)`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/glossary.html#term-parameter), [`Added in version 3.x`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/index.html), `Note  Warning  See also`, `Tables`, [`>>> examples`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/tutorial/interpreter.html#interactive-mode)

**In the editor:** [`help(obj)`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/functions.html#help), [`dir(obj)`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/functions.html#dir), [`sys.version`](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/sys.html#sys.version)
